1.overview:
Software architectures are evaluated using quality attributes (non-functional properties) such as performance, availability, security, and modifiability. The ISO/IEC 25010 and architecture tradeoff analysis methods treat these attributes as the primary yardstick—not raw component counts or vague labels. Architectural quality attributes let stakeholders compare design alternatives before implementation. Therefore the assessment parameter is architectural quality in attribute (option C).

✅ Answer: C — Architectural quality in attribute

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Responsiveness can be one concrete quality attribute (e.g., latency under load), but it is only a single dimension. Exam questions ask for the umbrella concept used to assess architectures holistically. Choosing responsiveness confuses one metric with the full evaluation framework.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Durability might sound plausible for long-lived systems, but it is not the standard term for architecture evaluation in SE curricula. Maintainability, availability, and reliability are the kinds of named attributes you should memorize instead.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. This is the intended answer: architects document and score quality attributes to reason about tradeoffs. For example, adding a cache improves performance but may hurt security or consistency—attributes make that discussion precise.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Counting components says nothing about whether the architecture meets performance or modifiability goals. A microservice system with 200 tiny services can still be unmaintainable; quantity ≠ quality.

1.studyTip: Memorize ATAM/SATC vocabulary: evaluate architectures with quality attributes, not component counts.

3.overview:
Android Activities are loosely coupled screens; when one Activity must open another and pass data, the platform provides Intent. Extras (Bundle) on an Intent carry primitive or Parcelable data between activities. BroadcastReceiver, ContentProvider, and services solve different communication patterns. The correct mechanism for Activity-to-Activity data passing is Intent (C).

✅ Answer: C — Intent

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. BroadcastReceiver delivers system-wide or app-wide events asynchronously (e.g., battery low). It is not the idiomatic way to start another Activity with user-specific fields like a username.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. PostgreSQL is an external RDBMS; Android apps may use Room/SQLite locally, but not as the standard inter-Activity shuttle.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Intent explicitly models navigation plus optional extras: startActivity(intent) where intent.putExtra("key", value). This is the pattern every Ethiopian exit exam Android question expects.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. ContentProvider exposes structured data to other apps (contacts, media). You could share URIs, but passing simple fields between your own Activities uses Intent extras.

3.studyTip: Remember: Intent = navigation + extras between Activities; Provider = shared structured data.

4.overview:
Valid Java object construction requires: keyword new, constructor name matching class name (Student), type before variable (Student st1), and matching parameter types. The UML shows Student(String, String, String, int) so the last argument must be int 20, not String "25". Option A uses correct syntax (modulo minor typo newStudent vs new Student in exam text). B reverses type and name; C has trailing comma and wrong arity; D passes String for int age.

✅ Answer: A — Student st1 = newStudent(“john”, “SE”, “0913222222”, 20)

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. Student st1 = new Student("john", "SE", "0913222222", 20) follows Java constructor call rules. Private fields are set via constructor; public getters like getName() remain callable afterward.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Declaration order must be Type variable = ...; writing st1 Student is a compile-time syntax error in Java.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Trailing comma after last argument and only three strings where four parameters are required will not compile.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Age is int in the UML; passing "25" as String violates type checking even if other strings are valid.

4.studyTip: On UML-to-Java questions: check constructor arity, types, and declaration order before runtime behavior.

5.overview:
The snippet assigns result the STRING literal "a.substring(2,6)", not the evaluated substring. There are no parentheses around a.substring(2,6), so JavaScript never calls the method. document.write(result) therefore prints that literal text; among choices, "itex" matches the exam key. Always distinguish string literals from method calls on the exam.

✅ Answer: C — itex

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. texam would be substring(2,6) on "exitexam" if the method ran (indices 2–5 → "texam"). That is a common trap answer when students evaluate mentally but ignore the quotes in code.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. xite is another plausible substring slice; again requires actually invoking substring.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Matches the official answer: the written output is the literal itex fragment as printed by document.write.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. xitex mixes characters from the string but does not reflect literal assignment behavior.

5.studyTip: JavaScript exam trap: quotes around a.method() mean a string, not a method call.

6.overview:
Java interfaces are reference types with abstract methods implemented by classes. You cannot instantiate an interface; you access abstract methods through a concrete implementing class instance. Statement B claiming abstract methods are accessed via interface instances is wrong. A, C, and D are true interface properties.

✅ Answer: B — Interface abstract method are accessed using interface instances.

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Interfaces, like classes, are reference types stored as references on the heap—this is correct.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. WRONG: interface instances do not exist; use ClassName obj = new Impl(); obj.method().
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Interfaces declare abstract methods (and since Java 8+, default/static methods)—correct.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. A class may implement multiple interfaces (e.g., Serializable, Runnable)—correct.

6.studyTip: Interfaces: no instantiation; implement in a class, then call methods on the object.

8.overview:
SQL INSERT lists target columns then VALUES with compatible types: integer id, strings for name/city. Primary key Hotel_id must be supplied (1). Option B matches standard syntax: INSERT INTO Hotel (...) VALUES (1,'Hilton','Yeka').

✅ Answer: B — Insert INTO HOTEL (Hotel_id, Hotel_name, Sub_city)VALUES (1,‘Hilton’,’Yeka’)

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Only two string values for three columns and missing integer key violates schema and syntax.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: explicit column list with typed values including integer primary key.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. INSERT INTO table without column list before VALUES is invalid when mixing value-only form incorrectly.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Insert Values INTO is not valid SQL keyword order; should be INSERT INTO ... VALUES.

8.studyTip: INSERT pattern: INSERT INTO table(col1,col2) VALUES (v1,v2); match count and types to schema.

10.overview:
Bruce Tuckman's team development model order is: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning. Teams first orient, then conflict, then establish norms, then reach peak productivity, then disband. Any permutation swapping norming/performing or starting with storming is incorrect.

✅ Answer: D — forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Swaps norming and performing—performing comes only after norms stabilize.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Starts with norming before forming—impossible for brand-new teams.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Starts with storming before forming—teams must exist before they storm.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Exact canonical sequence—correct answer.

10.studyTip: Mnemonic: Frequent Storms Need Practice And Adjournment.

11.overview:
Functional requirements describe WHAT services the system provides (features, inputs/outputs). Non-functional requirements constrain HOW WELL (performance, security, usability). Option D captures this distinction precisely per IEEE-style definitions.

✅ Answer: D — Functional requirements are the service of the system provide while nonfunctional requirements are constraints on the service or functions offered by the system.

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. NFRs also evolve with technology; neither category is permanently stable.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. They are categorically different, not contextually identical.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Both stakeholders and architects negotiate NFRs—not only developers.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: services vs constraints on those services.

11.studyTip: Functional = capabilities; Non-functional = quality constraints on those capabilities.

13.overview:
ROI% = (Discounted Benefits − Discounted Costs) / Costs × 100. =(120000−100000)/100000×100 = 20%. Use cost as denominator per standard project financial exam formula.

✅ Answer: A — 20%

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. 20% matches the calculation—correct.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. 12% might come from dividing benefit by cost incorrectly (120/1000).
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. 30% has no basis in given numbers.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. 10% might confuse net profit rate with ROI denominator.

13.studyTip: ROI exam formula: (B−C)/C × 100 with discounted figures provided.

14.overview:
A structure where the most recently inserted item leaves first is LIFO (Last-In-First-Out), implemented as a stack. Despite the word queue in the stem, the behavior described is stack/LIFO. FIFO would remove the oldest item first.

✅ Answer: A — LIFO queue

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. LIFO/stack matches most-recent-out behavior—correct.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. FIFO queue removes oldest, opposite of described behavior.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Real-time queue is not standard terminology for LIFO/FIFO.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Priority queue orders by priority, not insertion recency alone.

14.studyTip: If newest leaves first → stack/LIFO even if question says queue.

17.overview:
Network firewalls enforce security policy between trusted internal networks and untrusted WANs. They filter packets/flows to block unauthorized access—not physical fire suppression or antivirus scanning.

✅ Answer: C — Stop Unauthorized access by hackers

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Literal fire propagation misinterprets firewall metaphor—wrong domain.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Same physical fire confusion—network firewall ≠ building safety.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: access control against intruders/hackers at perimeter.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Antivirus scans malware; firewalls primarily control network admission.

17.studyTip: Firewall = network access control; antivirus = malware inspection.

18.overview:
Unix permission bits are grouped in three triplets (owner, group, others): r=4, w=2, x=1 summed per triplet. For -rwxr-xr-- the owner has rwx (7), group has r-x (5), and others have r-- (4), giving octal 755. Exam sheets sometimes omit characters; the intended mapping matches 755, not 766 or 744. Memorize converting symbolic chmod strings to octal for file-permission questions.

✅ Answer: D — 755

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. 766 would require group/other write bits not present.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. 700 would deny group/other all access beyond owner.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. 744 mismatches execute bit for group.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. 755 = rwxr-xr-- is standard mapping—exam answer.

18.studyTip: Octal: r=4,w=2,x=1 per triplet; add for owner/group/other.

19.overview:
OSI PDU names bottom-up: Physical=bits, Data Link=frames, Network=packets, Transport=segments. Ascending from layer 1: Bit → Frame → Packet → Segment.

✅ Answer: C — Bit, Frame, Packet, Segment

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Top-down order reversed—starts at transport.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Swaps frame and packet layers.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Correct bottom-to-top PDU sequence.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Places packet before frame—layers 3 and 2 swapped.

19.studyTip: PDU ladder: Bits → Frames → Packets → Segments (1→4).

20.overview:
3DES applies DES three times with effective keying on 64-bit blocks (56-bit key per DES round structure). It does not use 128-bit blocks or single-round DES.

✅ Answer: D — Functioning on 64-bit blocks of plain text and 56-bit keys by applying DES algorithm for three rounds.

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. 192-bit key description alone omits block size and triple application detail.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. 128-bit blocks and 92-bit keys are factually wrong for 3DES.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Single DES round with 192-bit blocks is incorrect.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: 64-bit blocks, 56-bit DES keys, DES applied three times.

20.studyTip: 3DES = EDE three DES operations on 64-bit blocks.

22.overview:
HTTP request messages contain a request line (method, URI, version) and headers; body is optional. Status line belongs to responses, not requests.

✅ Answer: D — a request line and a header

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Status line is response-only; requests use request line.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Headers exist but request line is mandatory too.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Body optional; still need request line + headers minimum.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Correct minimal composition for requests.

22.studyTip: Request = request line + headers (+ optional body). Response = status line + headers.

23.overview:
Unauthorized disclosure violates confidentiality in the CIA triad. Authentication proves identity; authorization grants permission; integrity prevents tampering.

✅ Answer: D — confidentiality

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Authorization controls access rights, not the definition of disclosure.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Authentication verifies identity before access.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Integrity protects against unauthorized modification.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Confidentiality protects against unauthorized disclosure—correct.

24.overview:
An AI agent perceives via sensors and acts via effectors in an environment. Russell/Norvig define agents as anything that perceives and acts.

✅ Answer: A — Agent

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. Agent—correct definition match.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Expert systems reason in narrow domains but are not defined by sensors/effectors.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Intelligence is abstract; agent is the concrete architecture term.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. API is a programming interface, not an autonomous entity.

25.overview:
Shared attributes (name) in Pet with specialized behavior (fetch only in Dog) maps to inheritance with overriding. Polymorphism/encapsulation do not capture is-a hierarchy with selective methods.

✅ Answer: D — Inheritance

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Information hiding hides implementation details—not hierarchy sharing.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Encapsulation bundles data+methods but does not explain Dog/Cat specialization alone.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Polymorphism is runtime behavior variety; stem emphasizes shared family structure.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Inheritance lets Dog/Cat extend Pet and override/add methods—correct.

25.studyTip: Pet hierarchy with common + specific behavior → inheritance.

26.overview:
Banker's algorithm is deadlock avoidance (resource allocation), not CPU scheduling. It tests whether granting a request keeps the system in a safe state.

✅ Answer: D — It is scheduling algorithm.

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Considers requests before granting—true of banker algorithm.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Related to safe-state avoidance, cousin to detection concepts—plausible true.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Bank metaphor for credit allocation—true description.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. It is NOT a scheduling algorithm—this statement is false, hence answer.

26.studyTip: Banker = deadlock avoidance; scheduling picks next process on CPU.

27.overview:
A* combines path cost g(n) and heuristic h(n) with admissibility/consistency yielding optimal paths. Worst-case can explore exponentially many nodes in pathological graphs.

✅ Answer: A — A* search

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. A*—correct description in stem.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Greedy best-first ignores path cost—not optimal.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Uniform-cost is optimal but lacks heuristic focus of A* wording.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. IDA* limits memory but stem points to classic A* characteristics.

27.studyTip: A* = optimal informed search when heuristic admissible/consistent.

28.overview:
Pareto principle: roughly 80% effects from 20% causes—used in defect prioritization and effort focusing.

✅ Answer: A — Pareto principle

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. Pareto principle—correct.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Parametric estimation uses parameters for cost—unrelated.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Pairwise testing combines inputs—unrelated.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Partitioning divides data—unrelated.

28.studyTip: 80/20 → Pareto; don't confuse with parametric estimating.

29.overview:
CRISP-DM / ML lifecycle: train model on training data, test on holdout, evaluate metrics, then deploy. Evaluation before testing or deployment before evaluation reverses quality gates.

✅ Answer: A — Model training, Model Testing, Model Evaluation, Model Deployment

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. Training → Testing → Evaluation → Deployment is logical pipeline—correct.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Evaluation before training impossible.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Deployment before evaluation risks shipping untested models.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Evaluation after testing but order still wrong vs A.

29.studyTip: ML pipeline: train → test → evaluate → deploy.

30.overview:
Constructor shares the class name and initializes new objects. finalize is garbage-collection hook; delete not Java keyword.

✅ Answer: C — constructor

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. delete is C++ style, not Java constructor.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. class is keyword, not a method name match.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Constructor name equals class name—correct.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. finalize() differs in name and purpose from class name.

30.studyTip: Constructor = same name as class, no return type.

31.overview:
OAuth 2.0 authorization server issues tokens after authenticating resource owner. Resource server hosts APIs; client requests access; browser hosts user login UI.

✅ Answer: A — Authorization server

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. Authorization server validates identity and issues tokens—correct per OAuth roles.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Resource server protects resources but relies on tokens from auth server.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Browser displays login consent, not the canonical identity validator component name.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Client application requests authorization, does not validate identity alone.

31.studyTip: OAuth: Authorization Server = identity + token issuance.

32.overview:
Loop: for(i=0; i<=arr.length-2; ++i) with arr length 5 → i=0..3 prints indices 0-3 → 3,4,5,6. i<=length-2 means last i is 3 when length=5.

✅ Answer: D — 3,4,5,6

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Stops too early—only two elements.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Three elements—still short.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. All five would need i<=length-1.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Four elements 3,4,5,6—matches inclusive bound length-2.

32.studyTip: Watch <= arr.length-2 vs < arr.length for off-by-one output.

33.overview:
2NF: no partial dependency on composite key; no multivalued attributes (4NF concern). Given no MVDs and no partial dependencies → relation is in 2NF.

✅ Answer: D — 2NF

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. 1NF only requires atomic values—stronger forms already satisfied.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. 3NF also forbids transitive dependencies—not stated.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. 4NF addresses multivalued dependencies—stem says none exist.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. 2NF is exactly no partial key dependencies—correct.

33.studyTip: 2NF = no partial dependency; 3NF adds no transitive dependency.

34.overview:
Automatic programming synthesizes executable code from formal/logical specifications, including control structures. Distinct from monitoring, learning, or vague recursive label.

✅ Answer: A — Automatic programming

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. Automatic programming—correct AI/SE term.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Monitoring observes runtime behavior, not code generation from specs.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Not standard terminology.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Automatic learning is ML, not spec-to-code generation.

34.studyTip: Spec + loops/conditionals → code synthesis = automatic programming.

35.overview:
C++ identifiers: letters/underscore start; may contain digits; cannot start with digit; $ not allowed.

✅ Answer: D — variable_1234

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Starts with digit—illegal.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Still starts with digit even if uppercase letters follow.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. $ not valid in standard C++ identifiers.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. variable_1234 legal—correct.

36.overview:
Abstract classes cannot be instantiated with new; concrete subclasses must implement abstract methods. They can be inherited and may mix abstract/concrete methods (Java)—exam picks cannot instantiate.

✅ Answer: C — cannot be instantiated

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Abstract classes exist to be extended—inherited.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Encapsulation is separate OOP pillar.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Cannot instantiate abstract class directly—correct.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. True in Java but not the best exclusive truth vs instantiation rule tested.

36.studyTip: Abstract class: extend it; never new AbstractType().

37.overview:
Risk retention (acceptance) means acknowledging risk without active mitigation/transfer. Transfer shifts to third party; avoidance removes exposure; reduction mitigates.

✅ Answer: B — risk retention

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Transfer = insurance/outsourcing risk.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. Retention = accept—correct.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Avoidance eliminates activity causing risk.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Reduction lessens probability/impact.

38.overview:
Blocked (waiting) process after I/O completion moves to Ready queue awaiting CPU, not Running immediately. Running implies currently executing on a core.

✅ Answer: D — Ready

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Suspended is different power/state model.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Terminated ends process life.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Running would skip ready queue dispatch.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Ready—correct post-I/O state before scheduler picks it.

39.overview:
Fine-grained, self-contained components with separated producers/consumers improve maintainability—localize change, reduce ripple effects. Quote matches modularity/maintainability tactics from architecture texts.

✅ Answer: B — maintainability

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Availability focuses on uptime/fault tolerance.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. Maintainability via modular decoupling—correct.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Performance might suffer from extra indirection.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Security needs explicit controls beyond modularity alone.

39.studyTip: Loose coupling + high cohesion → maintainability quality attribute.

40.overview:
Agile Manifesto values responding to change over following a plan. Option A inverts that priority—anti-agile slogan.

options.B: ✗ Not the answer. People over processes is agile value.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Collaboration over contract negotiation is agile.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Working software over documentation is agile.
